content: Antivenom immunoglobulins are not effective in all cases of snakebite envenoming. Therefore, comprehensive treatment must include antivenom therapy alongside other medical interventions such as cardiopulmonary and fluid resuscitation, airway intubation, mechanical ventilation, hemodialysis, wound debridement, reconstructive surgery, physiotherapy, and rehabilitation services. The involvement of wound care specialists, rehabilitation services, prosthetic limb manufacturers, and other recovery-focused professionals has been historically overlooked. Additionally, the psychological consequences of snakebite envenoming, such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and chronic depression, must be prioritized. The ultimate goal is to restore function and enable snakebite victims to return to healthy, productive lives. Addressing the challenges of improving the quality, safety, and cost-effectiveness of antivenoms is vital. Many countries face insufficient supplies of high-quality antivenoms, while poor-quality products and ineffective treatments have eroded public confidence in conventional healthcare. Strong engagement with communities and healthcare workers is necessary to encourage early care-seeking behavior, supported by coordinated health promotion strategies. Decades of neglect and inadequate regulation have led to the collapse of the antivenom market, characterized by low demand and an oversupply of substandard products, leaving millions of victims to suffer unnecessarily. At least three million effective treatments are needed annually, yet ensuring the safety, efficacy, and affordability of antivenoms remains a significant challenge. The World Health Organization (WHO) is working to establish the quality of antivenoms in sub-Saharan Africa and will collaborate with manufacturers to gather evidence of their safety and effectiveness. This program should be expanded to other regions where similar concerns exist, requiring thorough, independent investigation and validation. The cost of antivenom treatment varies widely, with incremental cost-effectiveness ratios for preventing deaths in West African countries ranging from $1,997 in Guinea-Bissau to $6,205 in Liberia and Sierra Leone. The cost per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted ranges from $83 in Benin to $281 in Sierra Leone, demonstrating that antivenom treatment is highly cost-effective compared to other health interventions. However, small-scale production results in high costs, discouraging investment. For example, in 2010–2011, approximately 83,000 treatments were supplied at an average cost of $124 per treatment, regardless of their effectiveness. The most effective product at the time cost $640 per treatment, a price unsustainable for large-scale supply. Investing in antivenoms can alleviate the suffering of victims and their families, enabling them to recover, rebuild their lives, and resume their roles as productive community members. This investment also aligns with SDG 1, which aims to end poverty, and the commitment to leave no one behind. WHO’s strategy emphasizes empowering communities, strengthening health systems, and ensuring access to safe, effective, and affordable medicines. By improving prevention, early care-seeking behavior, and treatment, more people will survive and recover from snakebites, contributing to healthier, more resilient communities. Snakebite envenoming disproportionately affects impoverished, rural populations in tropical and subtropical regions, where victims often lose their livelihoods, savings, and property due to the lack of effective treatment. This can lead to long-term economic hardship for individuals and their families. Investment in prevention and treatment not only saves lives but also reduces health inequities and economic losses. Snakebite envenoming also causes significant economic damage by killing or disabling livestock and working animals, further impacting vulnerable communities. WHO’s strategy for snakebite prevention and control includes empowering communities through education, communication, and training to make informed decisions about prevention and treatment. It also emphasizes the importance of engaging with local leaders, civil society, and health activists to improve outcomes. Operational research will be conducted to evaluate prevention strategies, and the findings will inform the development of affordable, context-appropriate interventions. Community-level education programs will be supported with technical guidance and learning materials. The strategy will be implemented in three phases: a pilot phase (2019–2020) in 10–12 high-burden countries, a scale-up phase (2021–2024) extending to 35–40 countries, and a full roll-out phase (2025–2030) to all affected countries. By fostering partnerships, improving market conditions, and increasing manufacturing capacity, the strategy aims to deliver three million effective treatments annually by 2030. Ultimately, the prevention and treatment of snakebite envenoming serve as a model for collaboration under the One Health approach, addressing both human and animal health. By investing in antivenoms and strengthening health systems, WHO aims to create a safer, healthier, and fairer world where all individuals can lead productive, fulfilling lives.
